title: Prosthetic heart valves: mechanical vs bioprosthetic selection, INR targets and anticoagulation
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Valvular Heart Disease)
2020 ACC/AHA Guidelines for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

steps.say: Choosing between mechanical and bioprosthetic heart valves balances thromboembolism against structural deterioration. Mechanical valves provide exceptional lifelong mechanical durability but require strict daily oral anticoagulation. Bioprosthetic tissue valves prevent lifelong anticoagulation but develop progressive structural calcification.
steps.tx: Prosthetic valve selection represents a critical trade-off between the lifelong durability of **mechanical valves** and the freedom from chronic anticoagulation offered by **bioprosthetic valves**. Mechanical devices require lifelong warfarin, whereas bioprostheses carry an inherent risk of **structural valve deterioration**. Selecting the optimal prosthesis requires thorough shared decision-making balancing lifelong anticoagulation risks against future reoperative hazards.

steps.say: Patient age serves as a primary guide for prosthetic valve selection. Guidelines recommend mechanical valves in patients under fifty years of age because tissue valves fail rapidly in young individuals. In patients older than sixty-five, bioprosthetic valves are preferred because life expectancy aligns with valve longevity.
steps.tx: Guideline consensus utilizes **patient age** to steer valve selection. Mechanical prostheses are favored in patients younger than 50 years to prevent reoperation, while bioprostheses are strongly recommended in patients older than 65 years where **structural deterioration rates** are significantly lower.

rows: Avoids high likelihood of multiple lifetime reoperations
Individualized balance of bleeding risk versus reoperation
Valve longevity exceeds patient actuarial life expectancy

steps.say: Vitamin K antagonist therapy with warfarin remains the only approved oral anticoagulant for mechanical valves. Modern direct oral anticoagulants such as dabigatran are strictly contraindicated. The RE-ALIGN trial proved that novel oral anticoagulants cause excessive thromboembolism and major bleeding in mechanical valve recipients.
steps.tx: Oral anticoagulation with the vitamin K antagonist **warfarin** remains the mandatory standard of care. **Direct oral anticoagulants** are contraindicated with mechanical prostheses because the landmark **RE-ALIGN trial** proved that dabigatran causes unacceptably high rates of mechanical thrombosis, arterial embolism, and excess major bleeding.

left.title: Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist)
points: Inhibits factors II, VII, IX, and X carboxylation
Proven safety and efficacy across mechanical valves

right.title: DOACs (Direct Thrombin / Xa Inhibitors)
points: RE-ALIGN trial demonstrated excess stroke and bleeding
Inadequate thrombin suppression on pyrolytic carbon

steps.say: International normalized ratio targets vary according to the anatomical valve position. The mitral position carries lower flow velocities, predisposing to thrombosis and requiring a target ratio of three point zero. An aortic mechanical prosthesis in a low-risk patient requires a lower target ratio of two point five.
steps.tx: Target anticoagulation levels depend on anatomical location. A mechanical **aortic valve target INR** is 2.5 in patients without thromboembolic risk factors. Conversely, a mechanical **mitral valve target INR** is 3.0 because lower velocity flow across the mitral orifice increases the hazard of **valve thrombosis**.

rows: AF, prior stroke, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable

steps.say: Bioprosthetic valves undergo progressive calcific degeneration over ten to twenty years. Macrophage infiltration and mineral deposition stiffen the glutaraldehyde-fixed leaflets, causing stenosis or tear-induced regurgitation. Modern valves incorporate specialized anti-calcification treatments to retard deterioration.
steps.tx: Tissue valves undergo inevitable **structural valve deterioration** within 10 to 20 years. Circulating calcium binds residual glutaraldehyde residues, leading to **calcific leaflet degeneration**, tissue stiffening, and tears culminating in symptomatic **prosthetic stenosis** or regurgitation that eventually requires surgical or transcatheter reintervention.

nodes.label: Phospholipid binding and calcium phosphate nucleation
Progressive leaflet stiffening, tears, and microcalcification
Late hemodynamic failure requiring valve intervention

steps.say: Catheter-based valve-in-valve procedures provide an alternative to high-risk repeat open surgery. Interventional teams deploy a transcatheter balloon-expandable valve inside the failed surgical bioprosthesis. This minimally invasive technique prevents repeat sternotomy in elderly and frail patients.
steps.tx: When a surgical bioprosthesis fails, a **transcatheter valve-in-valve** procedure provides a less invasive alternative to repeat sternotomy. The operator deploys a balloon-expandable transcatheter device directly within the **surgical sewing ring**, offering an effective alternative for **high-risk reoperations** with accelerated patient functional recovery.

left.title: Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve
points: Femoral transcatheter access avoids reoperative sternotomy
Dramatic reduction in hospital stay and perioperative recovery
Risks coronary ostial obstruction and elevated residual gradient

right.title: Redo Surgical Replacement
points: Complete explantation of old calcified prosthetic ring
Permits implantation of larger true orifice area
Carries higher operative morbidity and stroke risk

steps.say: Emergency management of mechanical valve thrombosis depends on hemodynamic stability and clot burden. Obstructive thrombosis causing shock mandates emergency surgical re-replacement or ultra-slow-dose intravenous thrombolysis. Cinefluoroscopy and transesophageal echocardiography assess leaflet motion and thrombus size.
steps.tx: Suspected obstructive **mechanical valve thrombosis** requires urgent evaluation with cinefluoroscopy and transesophageal echocardiography. Hemodynamically unstable patients in shock undergo emergency **surgical thrombectomy** or replacement, whereas select stable patients receive **slow-infusion thrombolysis** with tissue plasminogen activator under close continuous intensive monitoring.

nodes.label: Suspected prosthetic thrombosis: echo and cinefluoroscopy
Assess hemodynamic stability and NYHA functional class
Unstable/shock: emergency surgery or slow tPA infusion

steps.say: Pannus ingrowth represents a non-thrombotic cause of prosthetic valve obstruction. Dense perivalvular fibrous tissue proliferates from the annular sewing ring into the orifice. Unlike acute thrombus, chronic pannus produces slowly progressive gradients and requires surgical debridement or re-replacement.
steps.tx: Prosthetic obstruction can also result from **pannus formation**, a dense fibrous fibroelastic proliferation originating from the healing host annular bed. Distinguishing chronic, highly echogenic pannus from acute soft thrombus is vital, as pannus fails thrombolysis and requires **surgical re-replacement**. Differentiating pannus from thrombus dictates whether immediate operating room transfer for redo surgery is required or medical lysis should be attempted.

rows: Acute, sudden over hours to days
Slowly progressive over months to years
Soft, mobile mass with low acoustic impedance
Dense, highly reflective immobile fibrous tissue
